title: Analytic gradients for low-rank quantum optimal control
abstract: We introduce low-rank optimal control (LROC), a method for designing control pulses in open quantum systems whose full density-matrix simulation is prohibitively expensive. The method exploits a feature of quantum computing itself: because protocols are designed to preserve purity, the density matrix is dominated by a few pure states and admits an accurate low-rank factorization. LROC propagates only this factorized form and, by deriving the corresponding adjoint equation, obtains the gradient of any differentiable objective at the same reduced cost as the simulation, leading to a quadratic improvement in time and memory compared to the full master equation. We illustrate the breadth of the method on four superconducting-circuit tasks: preparation of a five-qubit GHZ state, a CNOT gate, qubit readout, and an error correction primitive, modeled with realistic multilevel transmons, decay, and strong drives, in each case reaching fidelities consistent with the intrinsic dissipation limits. LROC thereby extends pulse-level optimization to system sizes beyond the reach of existing gradient-based methods.
summary: This paper presents Low-Rank Optimal Control (LROC), a novel technique to optimize control pulses for open quantum systems like superconducting circuits. By exploiting the low-rank nature of the evolving density matrix, LROC calculates necessary gradients with significantly reduced computational cost compared to standard methods. This breakthrough extends gradient-based optimization to much larger and more complex physical systems.
main_problem: The primary challenge is designing optimal control pulses for open quantum systems where simulating the full density matrix evolution is computationally prohibitive.
main_result: The authors introduce Low-Rank Optimal Control (LROC), which achieves an analytic gradient calculation with a quadratic improvement in time and memory scaling compared to full master equation methods.
method: LROC combines the Low-Rank Approximation (LRA) of the density matrix ($\hat{ho} \simeq \Psi\Psi^\dagger$) with the adjoint state method, allowing for efficient gradient computation via an adapted Pontryagin maximum principle framework.
model_or_system: The work models open quantum systems using superconducting circuits (transmons), governed by a Lindblad master equation. The control Hamiltonian allows for time-dependent external driving fields.
key_observables: State preparation fidelity (e.g., GHZ state) and average gate fidelity (e.g., CNOT gate).
important_parameters: The low-rank approximation size ($M$) relative to the Hilbert space dimension ($N$), and the time step ($\Delta t$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that quantum protocols preserve purity, enabling the accurate low-rank factorization of the density matrix. The gradient derivation involves approximations in discretization.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the LROC algorithm flow: forward state propagation, loss calculation, backward adjoint evolution for gradients, and parameter update via gradient descent.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first establishing the low-rank master equation, then deriving the analytic gradient using the adjoint method (Weak Pontryagin maximum principle), and finally demonstrating its application to various physical tasks like state preparation and gate fidelity optimization.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant as it provides a scalable framework for optimizing quantum operations in realistic, dissipative hardware platforms by circumventing exponential scaling issues inherent in full density matrix simulations.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the LROC algorithm. A forward pass is evaluated with a candidate pulse and the states {Ψj} are stored in memory (blue block). From these, the loss is com- puted and the adjoint state is initialized and λ(T) evolves backward in time following Eq. (9) (red block), computing the gradient at every time tj = (j −1)∆t and subsequently discarding the forward state Ψj. The parameters are up- dated through gradient descent or Adam [34] and the process is repeated until convergence. A similar procedure holds for multi-state objectives by parallelizing over many states (faded dashed arrows). Further details on the numerical implemen- tation are provided in Appendix C 1.

FIG. 2. (a) Memory footprint and (b) total runtime as a func- tion of the Hilbert space dimension N for LROC (blue), AD with low-rank (purple), and AD with the full master equa- tion (red). (c) The accuracy of the gradient is controlled by ∆t and (d) M, with the latter hitting the plateau given by the trapezoidal error (dash-dotted gray lines). All plots are shown for a three-qubit GHZ state (see Sec. III A) where N is increased by increasing the Hilbert space dimension of the individual multilevel transmons and M = 2 [except for (d)]. The AD results were obtained with the Enzyme.jl [37, 38] package.
